document.title: Comments and Protest of Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc. in response to American Transmission Company LLC’s tariff filing

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
American Transmission Company, LLC 
) 
) 
) 
 
 
Docket No. ER26-3531-000 
COMMENTS AND PROTEST OF THE  
MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC. 
 
The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) submits1 these comments 
and protest in response to the proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC of MISO’s Open 
Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) filed by MISO as 
the Transmission Provider on behalf of American Transmission Company, LLC, by its corporate 
manager, ATC Management Inc. (collectively, “ATC”).  MISO appreciates the steps taken by 
ATC to expeditiously address the mandates of the Commission’s Order Instituting Proceeding 
Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act (“Show Cause Order”).2  MISO submits these 
comments and protest because ATC proposes Tariff changes related to the interconnection and 
operation of large loads in the ATC footprint that conflict with MISO’s pending Interconnection 
Reliability Requirements for Large Loads proposal (“IRR Proposal”).3  While MISO appreciates 
that the sequence and timing of MISO and ATC’s filings may be the underlying cause of the 
differences in ATC’s proposal and MISO’s IRR Proposal, MISO is concerned that ATC’s 
proposal, if accepted, would establish a separate large load framework rather than complementing 
 
1  
This submission is made pursuant to Rules 211 and 212 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.212 (2026). 
2  
Midcontinent Indep. System Op., Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”). 
3  
Ltr. To the Hon. Debbie-Anne Reese regarding the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s 
Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3600 (Aug. 28, 2026).

2 
a common MISO regional baseline consistent with ATC’s stated intent in its filing.4  Accordingly, 
MISO respectfully requests that the Commission direct ATC to revise Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
either to: (1) require ATC to submit revised Tariff sheets that adopt or integrate with MISO’s large 
load rules and procedures, remove redundant processes, and explicitly provide that any 
requirements imposed by Attachment FF-ATCLLC or ATC’s business practices on ATC Large 
Load are additional to those applicable to Large Load under the MISO Tariff and that, in the event 
of a conflict, the more restrictive rule governs; or (2) reject ATC’s proposal as unjust, 
unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory for large loads taking Transmission Service under the 
MISO Tariff.  
I. 
BACKGROUND 
MISO submits these comments and protest to resolve the mismatch in large load definitions 
and rules between MISO’s IRR Proposal and ATC’s proposed Tariff revisions.  This mismatch 
involves conflicting thresholds between the 100 MW large load threshold in ATC’s proposed 
Tariff revisions and the 50 MW large load threshold in MISO’s pending IRR Proposal, separate 
study processes, and related downstream impacts.  This issue appears to be a matter of timing 
resulting from the time lag between the issuance of the Show Cause Order, MISO’s request to hold 
those compliance directives in abeyance, ATC’s filing in this docket, and submission of MISO’s 
IRR Proposal.  
The Commission issued the Show Cause Order on June 18, 2026.5  The Show Cause Order 
directed MISO and the Transmission Owners to either: (1) show cause as to why MISO’s Tariff 
 
4  
Ltr. To the Hon. Debbie-Anne Reese regarding the American Transmission Company LLC’s Proposed Revisions 
to Attachment FF-ATCLLC of the MISO Tariff in Response to Show Cause Order, Docket No. ER26-3531 (Aug. 
28, 2026) at p. 2. 
5  
See Show Cause Order.

3 
remains just and reasonable without provisions addressing certain large load issues; or (2) explain 
what changes to the Tariff would address the Commission’s concerns, if the Commission were to 
determine that the Tariff has in fact become unjust and unreasonable.6  The Show Cause Order 
afforded MISO and the Transmission Owners 60 days to make their respective filing(s).7 
On August 3, 2026, MISO moved to hold all proceedings related to the Show Cause Order 
in abeyance for 90 days.8  The Abeyance Motion explained that MISO and the MISO Transmission 
Owners required additional time to continue the stakeholder process and submit FPA section 2059 
filings that address the concerns raised in the Show Cause Order.10  The Commission granted the 
90-day abeyance requested in the Abeyance Motion on August 14, 2026.11  ATC filed its proposed 
Tariff revisions three days later, on August 17, 2026.  MISO, in turn, filed the IRR Proposal on 
August 28, 2026.  
The mismatch in large load definitions and rules is understandable when viewed against 
this procedural backdrop.  At the time ATC filed its proposed Tariff revisions in this docket, the 
abeyance period had not expired, and MISO had yet to file its IRR Proposal and related large load 
threshold.  MISO believes this outcome was unintentional; after all, ATC’s filing states that ATC’s 
proposal is intended to be “complementary to MISO’s future filings” and to “work together with 
MISO’s process ….”12  The ATC proposal, however, asks the Commission to act on separate a 
 
6  
Id. at P 3.  
7  
Id. 
8  
Motion of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. and the MISO Transmission Owners to Hold 
Proceeding in Abeyance and Request for Shortened Comment Period and Expedited Treatment, Docket No. 
EL26-70-000 (Aug. 3, 2026) (“Abeyance Motion”).   
9  
16 U.S.C. § 824d.  
10  Abeyance Motion at 2.  
11  Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., et. al., 196 FERC ¶ 61,133 (August 14, 2026) (“Abeyance 
Order”). 
12  ATC Transmittal Letter at p. 2.

4 
separate large load framework for ATC instead of supplementing a common MISO regional 
baseline.  This raises practical and other challenges, including potential reliability impacts.  The 
appropriate solution in this instance is for the Commission to direct ATC to revise Attachment FF-
ATCLLC either to: (1) require ATC to submit revised Tariff sheets that adopt or integrate with 
MISO’s large load rules and procedures, remove redundant processes, and explicitly provide that 
any requirements imposed by Attachment FF-ATCLLC or ATC’s business practices on ATC 
Large Load are additional to those applicable to Large Load under the MISO Tariff and that, in 
the event of a conflict, the more restrictive rule governs; or (2) reject ATC’s proposal as unjust, 
unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory for large loads taking Transmission Service under the 
MISO Tariff. 
II. 
COMMENTS AND PROTEST 
A. 
ATC’s Proposal Is Contrary to its Stated Goal of Complementing MISO’s 
Large Load Framework. 
 
MISO appreciates that ATC’s goal is to provide a rule set that addresses concerns specific 
to large loads in the ATC footprint and that ATC intends for their proposal to complement MISO’s 
Large Load filings.  As ATC stated at the outset of its filing: 
ATC’s filing here is intended to establish requirements in its 
footprint and be complementary to MISO’s future filings. As 
described below, ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-
ATCLLC describe processes that are designed to work together with 
MISO’s process in the same way ATC’s local planning process in 
Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC 
works 
with 
the 
annual 
MISO 
Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) process today. ATC also 
seeks approval for modifications to the local planning process that 
is utilized today in ATC’s footprint.13 
 
 
13  ATC Transmittal Letter, at p. 2.

5 
MISO supports ATC’s stated goal and has long acknowledged the importance of allowing its 
Transmission Owners to establish additional or supplemental requirements in its footprint that 
work together with MISO’s Tariff rules.  Unfortunately, ATC’s proposed Tariff revisions may 
frustrate this goal and lead to unjust or unexpected outcomes for Large Load connecting to the 
MISO Transmission System.  This is because ATC’s proposed Tariff revisions create a different 
process with requirements that supersede MISO’s Large Load and Computational Load definitions 
and baseline reliability requirements for loads in the ATC footprint.   
Proposed Section V.F provides that “ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria and requirements 
established by ATCLLC’s Business Practices, as described herein, shall govern in ATCLLC’s 
footprint.”14  Taken together, these provisions create an entirely different rule set for large loads 
connecting to ATC’s transmission facilities—which are part of the MISO Transmission System 
and take Transmission Service pursuant to MISO’s Tariff—and purport to make the definitions, 
requirements, and studies that are or will be required by MISO’s Tariff for large loads inapplicable 
in the ATC footprint.  If the large load connects to the Transmission System through distribution 
facilities, including those built to support a large load, then ATC further proposes that its own cost 
allocation, study processes, readiness requirements, and forms of agreement will govern and that 
the requests for such interconnections will be processed by ATC rather than by MISO.15  Given 
 
14  Proposed Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC at Section V.F.  These include: (1) Steady State Criteria 
(including steady state voltage criteria); (2) Dynamic Stability Assessments; (3)  Resource Facility Requirements 
(including Voltage, Reactive Power, and Power Factor Control); (4) ATC Large Load Interconnection 
Requirements  (including Active Power Oscillations, Ramp Rate Limits, Voltage Ride Through, Load Power 
Factor)l and; (5) Large Load data monitoring, data retention, forecasting, and design criteria.  See, Proposed 
Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC at Section V.E 
15  Proposed Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC at Sections VI.A.1-VI.A12. Because ATC proposes to include 
many details of its rules in its business practice manuals, there is also a risk that new conflicts between ATC’s 
and MISO’s rules could arise as the rule sets develop.

6 
the broad sweep of these proposed rules, it is unclear what parts of MISO’s Large Load rules will 
still apply in ATC’s footprint and how conflicting requirements can be reconciled. 
 
MISO does not object to ATC developing supplemental rules and procedures needed to 
implement the rules contained in MISO’s Tariff in ATC’s footprint or to supplement MISO’s 
Tariff rules for Large Loads to the extent that ATC needs to impose additional reliability or 
operations requirements on ATC Large Load.  MISO welcomes ATC’s feedback on whether 
adjustments or additional flexibility is needed for individual requirements either included in the 
IRR Proposal or currently being developed in the Large Load Federal Power Act Section 205 
filings described in MISO’s Abeyance Request.  However, MISO is concerned that even with 
ATC’s good intentions to develop complementary processes, the proposed Tariff language 
describes an entirely separate rule set and creates a high risk of discordant rates, terms, and 
conditions for Transmission Service under the MISO Tariff for ATC Large Loads as opposed to 
those connecting to other parts of the MISO Transmission System.16  
B. 
ATC’s Proposal Is Impractical Because It Would Require ATC to Integrate 
ATC-Specific Requirements with MISO’s Broader Process. 
 
i. 
A uniform Large Load framework for the MISO Transmission 
System is necessary to establish a common regional reliability 
baseline. 
 
MISO’s Large Load reliability framework submitted in the IRR Proposal includes 
definitions, basic facility data, modeling, telemetry, forecasting, Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU), 
 
16  A similar concern applies to ATC proposal to maintain its own study process—the Generating Facilities 
Modification Notification (“GFMN”) Process separate from MISO’s Interconnection Procedures. See, ATC 
Transmittal Letter at p. 18.  As defined in ATC’s Tariff sheets, this process covers “modifications, retirements, 
suspensions, testing results, model updates, or other changes associated with a generating facility.”  See, Proposed 
Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC at Section IV (Definitions)—Generating Facility Modification 
Notification.  Unlike the Large Load provisions, ATC’s GFMN revisions do indicate that customers may also be 
subject to study processes under the Transmission Provider’s Tariff.  However, this still requires customers to 
undergo two separate study processes and it is not clear how conflicts would be resolved if ATC’s GFMN process 
reaches different conclusions regarding permissible changes or assigns different costs than those identified 
through MISO’s generating facility retirement, replacement, or material modification rules.

7 
ramp and ride-through requirements, as well as distinguishes Large Loads and Computational 
Loads with targeted requirements reflecting their specific reliability risks.  This is intended to 
provide a common regional reliability baseline and rule set that facilitates comparable treatment 
for Large Loads seeking to connect to all parts of the MISO Transmission System.  This uniformity 
both promotes fairness and will better expedite the development of large loads by promoting 
commercial certainty to Large Loads. 
Permitting ATC to implement different large load thresholds and accompanying rules for 
large loads interconnecting within the ATC footprint versus those interconnecting in the rest of the 
MISO region will create confusion and divergent reliability requirements within the MISO region.  
Ultimately, accepting ATC’s proposal as filed would fragment the MISO region and create an 
unlevel playing field for similarly situated loads seeking to interconnect to the MISO Transmission 
System as ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC extend beyond establishing local 
planning criteria resulting in disparate operational and economic treatment of loads interconnected 
to the MISO Transmission System.  ATC would impose a lower burden on Computational Loads, 
which—together with the higher threshold for load classification as a large load, could result in 
those loads realizing lower compliance costs than Large Loads in the rest of the MISO region by 
avoiding reliability requirements. 
ii. 
Granting ATC’s requested relief would create reliability 
coverage gaps. 
 
Large Loads could face a reliability coverage gap if ATC’s Large Load framework 
replaces, rather than supplements, MISO’s framework.  As noted, MISO defines Large Loads by 
applying a 50 MW threshold, whereas ATC Large Load applies a 100 MW threshold.  As such, 
Loads ranging from 50 MW to 100 MW in ATC’s footprint would be excluded from requirements 
applicable to comparable loads elsewhere in MISO.  This gap has significant  downstream impacts.

8 
MISO’s IRR Proposal explains that the 50 MW threshold defining Large Load is based on 
industry precedent and the need for a clear and administratively workable means of identifying 
significant, concentrated loads that warrant additional reliability visibility.17  A load of 50 MW is 
sufficiently large that its characteristics and behavior can be relevant to transmission planning and 
system operations.18  Because Large Loads above 50 MW increasingly exhibit dynamic operating 
characteristics and concentrated demand and utilize sophisticated power-electronic equipment and 
controls, additional facility information, telemetry, and modeling detail may be necessary to 
evaluate reliability impacts under both normal and contingency conditions.19  The data and 
modeling requirements in the IRR Proposal are intended to support reliable operation of the entire 
MISO Transmission System by improving the accuracy of planning assumptions, strengthening 
operational awareness, supporting disturbance analysis and model validation, and enabling more 
consistent evaluation of system performance associated with Large Load integration.20  As such, 
allowing ATC to apply the definition of ATC Large Load in the ATC footprint will have wide 
ranging impacts on reliability, system planning and operational awareness.  
ATC’s proposed 100 MW Large Load threshold would exempt 50–99 MW facilities—
including both traditional industrial loads and Computational Loads—from MISO’s day-ahead and 
real-time forecasting requirements.  These forecasts are essential inputs to MISO’s Reliability 
Assessment Commitment (RAC), Security Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED), Look-Ahead 
Commitment (LAC), and real-time dispatch processes. 
 
17  IRR Proposal, Testimony of B. Li, p. 12 (Aug. 28, 2026) (“Li Testimony”). 
18  Id. at p. 14. 
19  Id. at p. 24. 
20  Id.

9 
If ATC’s threshold replaces MISO’s 50 MW baseline in ATC’s footprint, a 75 MW load 
would provide no Large Load forecast submissions.  Because this data is needed for real time 
processes, MISO needs the ability to require this information directly from the Large Load in real 
time in order to anticipate demand swings, commit generation reliably, maintain reserve 
sufficiency, and manage real time system balance.  
MISO’s concern does not end at the 100 MW threshold.  Because ATC proposes to 
supersede MISO’s requirements, even a 100+ MW Large load connected through ATC 
transmission facilities would still be excused from MISO’s requirements, including the 
requirement to provide data to MISO in real time.21 
If the ATC Large Load definition is accepted, neither MISO’s nor ATC’s requirements 
would apply to a 75 MW Computational Load.  This load source could fall outside MISO’s 
targeted the Phasor Measurement Unit / high-resolution measurement requirements.  If an 
oscillation occurs in the area with the 75 MW load, failure to apply large load data monitoring and 
communication rules would prevent MISO from performing the synchronized measurements 
needed to determine whether the load is the source, contributing to the oscillation, or responding 
to it.  This makes source identification and mitigation more difficult, impacting Transmission 
System reliability. 
This problem is compounded for Computational Loads.  MISO applies targeted modeling 
and PMU requirements to Computational Loads to address their distinct dynamic and oscillatory 
risks.  ATC does not appear to establish an equivalent separate classification, potentially resulting 
 
21  Many of MISO’s Large Load rules focus on facilitating real-time visibility into how large loads are operating in 
order to gauge system-wide effects and potential responses. Even if ATC is correct that 100 MW is an appropriate 
threshold for their facilities, the concern remains that their proposal would leave an ATC-shaped hole in MISO’s 
real-time view of Large Loads on the MISO Transmission System. ATC may ultimately require reporting from 
the large load to ATC.  But even good collaboration and data sharing between ATC and MISO cannot fully 
substitute for instantaneous communications directly between the large load and MISO’s systems.

10 
in different requirements for similar loads based on where they interconnect.  This disconnect 
imposes challenges because Computational Loads often exhibit highly coordinated, rapid demand 
swings and power-electronic dynamics that can impact the entire MISO Transmission System.22  
If MISO cannot apply its Large Load data and visibility requirements and Computational Load 
classification to loads connecting through ATC transmission facilities, this would further inhibit 
MISO’s ability to anticipate demand swings, commit generation reliably, maintain reserve 
sufficiency, and manage real time system balance to account for loads whose impact shifts 
definitionally can be sudden and significant given their size.  
ATC’s proposal raises broader reliability concerns that extend throughout the MISO 
region.  Load loss, ride-through/recovery, and oscillatory behavior do not remain confined within 
ATC’s footprint; they can affect frequency, voltage, nearby generation, and system stability across 
MISO.  ATC’s transmission facilities are part of the larger MISO Transmission System, and the 
electrical impacts of discordant rules cannot be limited to just ATC’s facilities. 
iii. 
Implementing ATC’s Proposal would Create Gaps and 
Misalignments with Downstream MISO Processes.  
 
In addition to different definitions, thresholds, and recipients of large load data, ATC 
proposes to formalize certain business practices “containing policies, practices, and requirements 
directed specifically at large loads” that are identified on its website without a discussion of how 
 
22  MISO’s IRR Proposal includes a definition of Computational Load to distinguish a subset of Large Loads that 
may exhibit operational characteristics different from more traditional loads, including rapid changes in demand, 
highly coordinated control behavior, and power-electronic responses during system disturbances.  This distinction 
allows MISO to apply certain incremental requirements—such as ramp, PMU, and ride-through requirements—
only where those characteristics warrant additional reliability consideration to preserve reliable operations beyond 
the ATC footprint. Events involving ramp and ride-through requirements can impact the entire MISO 
Transmission System. Defining Computational Load therefore supports a more targeted and risk-informed 
approach, rather than applying the same requirements to all Large Loads regardless of facility type or operating 
behavior.  Li Testimony at p. 13.

11 
they will complement MISO’s business practices manuals.23  These include a form of application 
specific to large loads connecting to the MISO Transmission System through ATC transmission 
facilities, their own study procedures, and their own transmission service agreement. 24  Allowing 
these separate processes creates disconnects with other downstream processes that MISO is 
charged with implementing.   
For example, MISO is charged with providing Transmission Service under a single Tariff.25  
As the Commission acknowledged in the Show Cause Order, many of the rules and procedures 
needed to accommodate large loads will be made applicable through transmission service 
processes imposing obligations on an Eligible Customer taking service to provide energy to the 
large load.26  MISO currently is developing revisions to Tariff rules governing transmission service 
processes and products responsive to the Show Cause Order through its Large Load 205 filings.  
Leaving aside any fairness implications of granting the same transmission services to Eligible 
Customers with divergent study and operational requirements, it is unclear from a practical and 
procedural prospective, how these rules would be implemented if MISO is not the entity that 
receives the application or operational assumptions that underlie transmission service options may 
not apply to the large load.  MISO does not object to ATC’s implementation of large load 
requirements in addition to the baseline established in MISO’s IRR Proposal e.g., if ATC were to 
 
23  ATC Transmittal Letter, at p. 5. 
24  ATC Transmittal Letter, at p. 14.  Transmission Owners Agreement, Appendix I, Section 7.1.  
25  See Agreement of Transmission Facilities Owners to Organize the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, 
Inc.. (“Transmission Owners Agreement”) Appendix I, Section 7.1 (Service under the Tariff. Customers will 
receive transmission service under a single Tariff which will apply to transmission service over the entire MISO 
Region (including the ITC), subject to changes to the Tariff accepted by FERC that the ITC may propose pursuant 
to this Appendix I. Customers will apply for service on the MISO OASIS. MISO will execute the agreements 
with the customers for service and studies. The ITC shall make all decisions on rate discounts for ITC-only 
transactions.). 
26  Show Cause Order at PP 1(noting the distinction between large loads and Eligible Customers) and 13 (discussing 
the “…need for clear and consistent tariff provisions regarding the provision of transmission service to Eligible 
Customers on behalf of large loads”).

12 
propose to use the 100 MW load threshold as a trigger for additional requirements in its footprint, 
but that is not the proposed Tariff languages does.  Rather the point is that a uniform baseline 
process is needed both to create space for complementary ATC-specific planning criteria and 
ensure that any required processes appropriately connect with downstream MISO processes. 
C. 
Granting This Protest Is Consistent with ATC’s Stated Intent.  
 
Granting this limited protest would align with ATC’s statements in its filing.  ATC states 
that ATC’s proposal is intended to be “complementary to MISO’s future filings” and “designed to 
work together with MISO’s process in the same way ATC’s local planning process in Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC works with the annual MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) process 
today.”27  ATC’s proposed Tariff redlines, however, state that ATC requirements “shall govern” 
in its footprint and indicates ATC may selectively defer requirements to MISO.28  This provides 
too much uncertainty to Large Loads and results in inconsistent Large Load requirements.   
MISO is willing to work with ATC to establish incremental criteria in the ATC region that 
will complement MISO’s baseline reliability framework.  MISO also understands that ATC made 
its filing in response to the Show Cause Order, in advance of the submission of MISO’s IRR 
Proposal, and without time to fully coordinate its proposed framework with MISO.  Now that both 
parties have filed their respective proposals, there is time for the parties to work together to address 
the needs of the region while acknowledging that ATC may need to impose requirements on large 
loads that are in addition to the baseline reliability requirements established in the IRR Proposal. 
MISO is sensitive to the challenges that ATC faces in filing supplemental requirements 
that are responsive to needs in the ATC footprint while aligning with MISO processes that are still 
 
27  ATC Transmittal Letter at p. 2.   
28  ATC Tariff Redlines at p. 21 (“The ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria and requirements established by ATCLLC’s 
Business Practices, as described herein, shall govern in ATCLLC’s footprint.”).

13 
in development.  This is a difficult task and both MISO and ATC are working to develop new rules 
on accelerated schedules.  To address this issue and better facilitate coordination, MISO suggests 
that the Commission require ATC to make a future compliance filing no earlier than the date by 
which MISO will make its Large Load 205 filings---i.e., November 16, 2026, or the date on which 
the Commission acts on MISO’s IRR filing, whichever is later.  Such a compliance period would 
align MISO and ATC’s development schedules and allow ATC to see (and participate in 
developing) the base rule set before it files supplemental requirements.  Such alignment will have 
long term benefits for ATC and MISO’s large load customers by avoiding rule conflicts, process 
redundancies, or unduly disparate treatment of large loads. 
III. 
COMMUNICATIONS 
MISO requests waiver of Rule 203(b)(3)29 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and 
Procedure to the extent necessary to permit the designation of more than two persons for service 
on behalf of MISO in this proceeding and requests all communications related to this filing be

14 
IV. 
NOTICE AND SERVICE 
MISO has served a copy of this filing electronically, including attachments, upon each 
person designated on the official service list compiled by the Secretary as well as on all Tariff 
customers, MISO Members, Member representatives of transmission owners and non-
transmission owners, as well as all state commissions within the MISO Region and the 
Organization of MISO States.  The filing has been posted electronically on MISO’s website at 
https://www.misoenergy.org/legal/ferc-filings/ for other interested parties in this matter. 
V. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, MISO respectfully requests that the Commission direct ATC to revise 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC either to: (1) require ATC to submit revised Tariff sheets that adopt or 
integrate with MISO’s large load rules and procedures, remove redundant processes, and explicitly 
provide that any requirements imposed by Attachment FF-ATCLLC or ATC’s business practices 
on ATC Large Load are additional to those applicable to Large Load under the MISO Tariff and 
that, in the event of a conflict, the more restrictive rule governs; or (2) reject ATC’s proposal as 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory for large loads taking Transmission Service under 
the MISO Tariff. 
Respectfully submitted, 
/s/ Christopher D. Supino
